explain.text:
Numbers below zero are negative numbers. Think of a thermometer as a number line stood on end. Higher up is always bigger, so −5 °C is warmer than −18 °C, even though 18 is more than 5. Getting the sign right matters too, because reefer cargo claims have come from mixing up plus and minus temperatures.[^1]

A zero is not always nothing. Many pressure gauges read 0 at the pressure of the air around them, and a pressure below that counts as negative.[^2] A minus can also mean the other way round. A digital meter on DC volts shows a minus when its probes touch the opposite terminals.[^3] 3 and −3 are opposites, the same distance either side of zero.

**Higher up is bigger, so the further below zero a number sits, the smaller it is.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** Higher up the line is bigger. The bigger the number after the minus, the further below zero it sits, so the smaller it is.

**Worked example:** Say three cold rooms read −12 °C, −18 °C and −29 °C. The least cold is the warmest, the one nearest the top, so −12 °C. The coldest is −29 °C, lowest of all.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading −18 as bigger than −5 because 18 is more than 5. On the line −18 sits lower, so it is smaller and colder.
- Taking a negative reading for a fault. A meter on DC volts that reads 12.0 V reads −12.0 V with its leads the other way round.

sources.title: The Carriage of Reefer Containers - West of England P&I Club
sources.quote: Many reefer container cargo claims have arisen due to confusion between the Fahrenheit and Celsius temperature scales, and also between positive (+) and negative (-) temperatures.

sources.title: 11.6 Gauge Pressure, Absolute Pressure, and Pressure Measurement - College Physics 2e | OpenStax
sources.quote: Gauge pressure is the pressure relative to atmospheric pressure. Gauge pressure is positive for pressures above atmospheric pressure, and negative for pressures below it.

sources.title: How to Measure DC Voltage with a Digital Multimeter | Fluke
sources.quote: Just recognize if the probes touch opposite terminals, a negative symbol will appear in the display.

checks.label: Higher up is bigger: −2 > −7, −5 > −18, −12 > −18 > −29 and 1 > −0.5 > −3/4 > −2. As drawn, −5 °C sits above −18 °C and −12 °C above −18 °C above −29 °C; and each puzzle accepts only its right answer

Places: −3 is 3 steps below 0 and 3 is as far above it; −3/4 is the third of four quarter ticks below 0; the gauge marker 3 tenth-steps below 0 reads −0.3 bar, not −0.7; 12 and −12 are opposites, drawn the same distance either side of 0
A slid tag lands on the nearest whole step and stays on the line: 2.4 steps down from 0 lands on −2, 2.6 on −3, and past either end it stops at the end
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends, hops at least 0.2 s apart, and every answer's motion within 2.5 s

applied.problem: 'Getting this right matters' ties ordering −5 and −18 to claims the quote blames on sign mix-ups, and its 'many' also covers Celsius/Fahrenheit; 'a pressure gauge … reads negative' fits only gauges made to read below 0; the minus shows on a digital meter on DC, the source's case.
On AC a meter shows no minus when its leads are swapped, so the mistake needs the DC case its source is about; the cold-room readings are values chosen for the example and should be worded as chosen.
The temperatures, pressures and voltages on the screens are values chosen for the puzzles, not measurements, but nothing in the spec says so; the screens' own caption does.

notes.problem: Every number is listed as kind 'constant' with no source, but all are values chosen for the screens (−3, −2, −5 °C, −18 °C, −0.6 bar, −0.3 bar, −12 V, the cold rooms); they are 'assumed' under the number rule.
